statement: Vessel class on this trade: Capesize.

statement: Vessel class on this trade: Panamax.
quote: U.S. grain cargoes are carried aboard vessels of the Panamax size or smaller, with capacity of 90,000 DWT or less, as a result of terminal constraints in both the U.S. and Asia.
note: All US grain exports, not PNW-Japan specifically.

statement: Vessel class on this trade: Panamax.
quote: Given the relatively short distances for most of the trade, smaller vessel segments dominate. The segments smaller than panamaxes have carried around three-quarters of the grain exports from the region, with handysize vessels accounting for the largest share.
note: All Black Sea grain exports (Signal Ocean, last four years); the same paragraph names Egypt as the leading destination.

statement: Vessel class on this trade: Supramax.
quote: The reduction, held across every week of the window, concentrated the remaining programme on Novorossiysk and fell most heavily on Handysize and Supramax employment.
note: Russian wheat loadings at the four deep-sea Black Sea terminals (Signal, five weeks to 28 August 2026), all destinations. Breakwave (pages/b3_breakwave-blacksea.txt) gives Handysize as the largest share of Black Sea grain overall.

statement: Vessel class on this trade: Panamax.
quote: At current volumes, Argentina's participation does not materially change the existing Panamax and Supramax percentage shares. However, if buyers adopt smaller parcel sizes or adjust scheduling, Supramax utilization could gradually increase. A key operational factor is Argentina's inland export system - most agricultural exports transit the Paraná-Paraguay waterway to the Rosario hub, where draft limitations can require partial loading at deeper-water ports.
note: Written about Argentine wheat to China, not soy; the preceding sentence gives China-bound wheat as ~70% Panamax / ~20% Supramax (all origins).

statement: Vessel class on this trade: Supramax.
quote: Fertilisers are the commodity I traded most at Maersk Broker in the Supramax segment. The trade flows follow agricultural calendars: potash from Canada (Vancouver) and Belarus/Russia (Baltic ports) to importers in South Asia, Southeast Asia, and Latin America; phosphate from Morocco (Jorf Lasfar) and the Western Sahara to Asia; urea from the Middle East (Jubail, Mesaieed) and China to global agricultural markets.
note: Broker blog; names urea from Mesaieed within the Supramax segment but to 'global agricultural markets', not Brazil specifically. Breakwave (2024-08-02, pages/b3_breakwave-bigpic2024.txt) notes Panamax growth on Oman-Brazil fertiliser exports (different origin).

statement: Vessel class on this trade: Supramax.
quote: A charterer booking a grain voyage from the Black Sea to a Mediterranean grain receiver, or a fertiliser shipment from Jubail to an Indian coastal terminal, will typically fix a Supramax
note: Broker blog; Jubail (Saudi Arabia) to an Indian coastal terminal, not Ruwais-Mundra.

statement: Vessel class on this trade: Panamax.

note: Heading on the line above: 'Canada (Vancouver) → China (sulphur / potash)'. Aggregator. BC Government (2011, pages/b3_bcgov-potash.txt): Canpotex's U-SEA COLONSAY 'capable of carrying approximately 60,000 tonnes of potash' serving Asia.

statement: Published transit time: approximately 47 days.

statement: Average sailing speed of oil tankers: 11.4 knots (2024).
quote: However, most other sectors experienced declines. The average speed of oil tankers dropped slightly (-0.4% to 11.4 knots), with larger decreases recorded among bulk carriers (-0.8% to 10.9 knots), car carriers (-0.9% to 15.0 knots), and large LPG carriers (-1.2% to 13.9 knots).
note: 2024 annual figure, provided only because no 2025 crude-tanker figure was found. Covers all oil tankers (crude and products).

statement: Average sailing speed of product tankers: 11.2 knots (January-February 2025).
quote: In the first two months of 2025, the average sailing speed of LNG carriers decreased by 2.0% to 14.6 knots compared to the average recorded in 2024; that of bulk carriers by 1.7% to 10.7 knots; and that of product tankers by 1.1% to 11.2 knots.
note: Percentage differs between relays (Manteniship/San Simon: -1.1%; Splash247: -1.7%) but the 11.2 knots figure is the same.

statement: Average sailing speed of LNG carriers: 14.6 knots (January-February 2025).
quote: In the first two months of 2025, the average sailing speed of LNG carriers decreased by 2.0% to 14.6 knots compared to the average recorded in 2024; that of bulk carriers by 1.7% to 10.7 knots; and that of product tankers by 1.1% to 11.2 knots.
note: Clarksons Research figure relayed by trade press; covers only the first two months of 2025, not the full year. Same figures in Splash247 (2025-03-10, pages/splash-speeds.txt) and San Simon & Duch (pages/lsansimon-1.txt). No full-year 2025 figure found in public sources; the Clarksons original (Creedon, 'Vessel speeds: On the way down', 7 March 2025, cited in UNCTAD RMT 2025) is paywalled.

statement: Average sailing speed of bulk carriers: 10.7 knots (January-February 2025).
quote: In the first two months of 2025, the average sailing speed of LNG carriers decreased by 2.0% to 14.6 knots compared to the average recorded in 2024; that of bulk carriers by 1.7% to 10.7 knots; and that of product tankers by 1.1% to 11.2 knots.
note: All bulk carriers; no Capesize-specific 2025 average found. Same source says eco VLCCs and Capesizes sail about half a knot faster than conventional ships (no absolute figure).

statement: Average sailing speed of container ships: 14.7 knots (2025 year-to-date (to December 2025)).
quote: Furthermore, despite increased port congestion, capacity-weighted average sailing speed has year-to-date 2025 fallen to 14.7 knots from 14.8 knots in 2024. Speeds, however, remain elevated compared to the 14.4 knots in 2023.
note: BIMCO capacity-weighted average, not Clarksons; methodology differs from the Clarksons 2024 figure of 14.0 knots.
